extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political philosophy, constitutional theory, and law
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and principles for when executive, parental, political, despotical powers, and conquest are legitimate or illegitimate; addresses prerogative, limits of authority, and rights of the conquered and innocents. Useful for evaluating claims about lawful power and the justification for government actions or resistance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative (executive discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: The power to act according to discretion for the public good, without prescription of law and sometimes even against it; exercised where municipal law gives no direction and for cases which cannot be safely foreseen by law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prerogative is legitimate only while employed for the benefit of the community and suitably to the trust and ends of government; its exercise is judged by its tendency to the good or hurt of the people. Examples: mitigating rigid laws, pardoning some offenders, acting in emergencies (e.g., not pulling down an innocent man's house to stop a fire next door). Antipattern: using prerogative to set up a separate or unequal interest distinct from the public good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive adjustment of representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the executive has the power of convoking the legislature, it may regulate numbers or create representatives in places that have a just right to be represented in proportion to the assistance they afford the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such adjustments, if made to restore fair and equal representation and for the public good, are not establishing a new legislature but restoring the true one; they justify themselves when they bring representation nearer to equality and the original frame of government. Antipattern: altering representation in ways that tend to injure, oppress, or establish unequal subjection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitation of prerogative by positive law is not encroachment
rubrics_metrics.description: When the people by express laws define or limit prerogative in points where it was formerly left indefinite, they do not wrongfully encroach on prince's rights but declare how that power ought be used for the public good.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: People may and should constrain prerogative where its former indefinite exercise has been abused; restricting prerogative to prevent private ends is proper, not an encroachment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Who judges improper use of prerogative (remedy when no earthly judge)
rubrics_metrics.description: If executive or legislative power is used to enslave or destroy the people and there is no earthly judge because legislature depends on the executive, the people have no earthly remedy and must appeal to a higher right (an appeal to heaven).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'appeal to heaven' (i.e., judgement by the people, potentially including resistance or revolution) is legitimate when the inconvenience or injury is such that the majority feel compelled to remedy it; it is not a license to perpetual disorder but a last resort when no earthly redress exists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paternal (parental) power: scope and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Paternal power is that which parents have over their children to govern them for their good until they reach the use of reason; it is natural and corrective, not arbitrary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parental power does not extend to life and death or to unlimited control of the child's property once grown; it exists only during minority to supply inability and instruct the child. Antipattern: treating parental authority as political or despotical power over adult children.

rubrics_metrics.name: Political power: origin, purpose, and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Political power is that which individuals in the state of nature give up into the hands of society and governors by compact or consent, with the explicit trust that it will be used for the people's good and preservation of property, lives, and liberties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Its end and measure are the preservation of members of the society; it cannot be absolute arbitrary dominion over lives and fortunes, but a power to make laws and penalties necessary to preserve the whole. Origin lies only in compact and mutual consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Despotical power: legitimate source and extent
rubrics_metrics.description: Despotical power is absolute arbitrary power one man has over another (to take away his life when he pleases), arising not from nature or compact but from forfeiture—i.e., from putting oneself in a state of war by unjust violence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Despotical power is only justifiable over those who have forfeited their rights by violent aggression; it cannot be conferred by compact and does not apply to those who have not renounced their reason or engaged in war.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction among paternal, political, and despotical power
rubrics_metrics.description: These are distinct species of authority: paternal power applies to children in minority, political power arises from consent to preserve property and society, and despotical power arises only from forfeiture (state of war).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claims about authority by identifying which category they fall into and applying the respective limits: paternal < political < despotical in extent and justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conquest does not of itself found legitimate government
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest, being mere force, cannot erect a new legitimate government without the consent of the people; the aggressor who unjustly invades another's rights gains no rightful title over the conquered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extortion by force (even by crowned rulers) is no different in moral right from robbery; promises or obligations extorted by force bind not at all. Conquest may enable a new frame only if the people freely consent to it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on conqueror's power over persons
rubrics_metrics.description: A conqueror's legitimate power extends only over those who joined in the unjust war (whose lives, having been forfeited by aggression, are at the victor's mercy) and not over innocents who did not concur in the aggression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Those who did not participate retain their freedom; the conqueror cannot lawfully subject entire peoples who did not commit the wrong. If conqueror compels submission by force, that does not create rightful obligation without consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on conqueror's rights over property
rubrics_metrics.description: Conquest does not give an absolute right to the possessions, lands, or posterity of the conquered; the right at most extends to reparations for damages and charges of the war, and must preserve the subsistence claims of innocent wives and children.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The conqueror may appropriate goods to make reparation but cannot legitimately seize the entire inheritance or dispossess posterity; damages of war seldom justify permanent dispossession of land. If reparations and children's maintenance conflict, preservation of innocents takes precedence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Extorted promises and obligations are void
rubrics_metrics.description: Promises, deeds, or transfers obtained by force do not create binding obligations; what is gotten by force remains the right of the original owner and ought to be restored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: a person forced at dagger-point to convey estate retains the right and may resume it; similarly, money handed under duress does not extinguish original rights. Antipattern: treating forced concessions as valid consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of prerogative in infancy of government and historical precedent
rubrics_metrics.description: In early or small commonwealths, many matters were left to rulers' discretion and government was mostly prerogative; where rulers used prerogative visibly for public good, people acquiesced and prerogative expanded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical enlargement of prerogative under good rulers does not create an unlimited right for successors; precedent of beneficial acts does not justify later harmful uses of presumed prerogative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental law of nature: preservation of all
rubrics_metrics.description: A paramount law antecedent to all positive law is that all members of society are to be preserved as much as may be; this principle justifies mitigation of law, pardon, and certain prerogative actions in emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When strict enforcement of laws would harm preservation (e.g., strict application causing greater harm), executive discretion to deviate is warranted. Use this principle to weigh acts of mercy, pardon, or extraordinary executive measures.
